doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

chapter: Radio, the Jazz Institute and Kenton
title: Musicians versus what has been written about them
summary: Poston says West Coast musicians were dismissed by critics, and Mulligan, Rogers and Paich differed from their reputations.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I had the same experience, you know at SUNY Fredonia. He came there and I was star- struck and I kept thinking that’s what I want to do. I want to be in a band like that. And as it turns out, you know, I’m more of a Basie guy. But still, there’s nothing like that. I’m wondering if, in all your research that you’ve done about different people, especially on the West Coast, and you read what other people write about them, and then you get to know the actual person and you have conversations about them. Have you come across instances where what the actual person says refutes what has been written about them?

Many times. Many times. Because as you know the West Coast scene of the ‘50s, by the end of the ‘50s there was a definite turning point within the critics and people writing about it where that music was very much dismissed and artists associated with that music got a lot of negative press as well. And so then I would — as doing the research, and you would read things, like you said, you would read these interviews and things about certain artists that just didn’t — when I would meet them and get to know them it didn’t add up at all. Even Gerry Mulligan. You know Gerry you know had this reputation, as you know, was temperamental and this and that and the other, and he was never like that with me at all. Now to be honest, I saw that side but not like people had described it. But Shorty Rogers, sweetest guy in the world, very easygoing. Marty Paich, very difficult
